name: Phrasal Verbs and Proverbs for Spoken English

cards.meaning: To mention or introduce a topic in conversation
cards.examples:
I didn't want to bring up the bug in the sprint review.
She brought up a great point about code reusability.
Can we bring up the deployment issue in tomorrow's standup?
He brought up the idea of switching to a microservices architecture.
Someone finally brought up the question of team bandwidth.

cards.meaning: To continue doing something despite difficulties
cards.examples:
Even with the server down, we carried on testing locally.
Let's carry on with the meeting — the manager will join late.
She carried on working even after the deadline was pushed back.
We need to carry on refactoring despite the pressure to ship.
Carry on with what you were doing; I'll handle this issue.

cards.meaning: To reach the same level as others; to update with someone
cards.examples:
I missed the design review — can you catch me up?
Let's catch up over coffee and talk about the project status.
I need to catch up on the tickets I missed during leave.
She caught up with the new tech stack over the weekend.
Can we catch up after the standup to discuss the blockers?

cards.meaning: To briefly report on status or confirm with someone
cards.examples:
I'll check in with the QA team to see where things stand.
Can you check in by EOD and let me know the progress?
We check in every morning to share what we're working on.
I just wanted to check in and see if you need any help.
She checked in with the client before pushing the final release.

cards.meaning: To find or encounter something unexpectedly
cards.examples:
I came across a really useful Stack Overflow answer for this bug.
You came across as very confident in the technical interview.
She came across an interesting article on AI ethics.
We came across a performance bottleneck during load testing.
He came across poorly in the meeting because he wasn't prepared.

cards.meaning: To think of or create an idea or solution
cards.examples:
We need to come up with a better caching strategy.
She came up with a clever workaround for the legacy API.
Can you come up with a rough estimate for this feature?
The team came up with three options for the system architecture.
I couldn't come up with a good name for the variable.

cards.meaning: To reduce the amount of something
cards.examples:
We need to cut down on the number of unnecessary API calls.
I'm trying to cut down on meetings by using async updates.
The new linter helps us cut down on code style issues.
Let's cut down on technical debt before adding new features.
The team cut down on bugs by writing more unit tests.

cards.meaning: To handle, manage, or take care of a problem or situation
cards.examples:
I'll deal with the production issue right away.
She dealt with the angry client very professionally.
We need to deal with the security vulnerability before shipping.
How do you deal with conflicting priorities in your day?
He dealt with three critical bugs before lunch.

cards.meaning: To fail to keep up with a schedule or standard
cards.examples:
We're falling behind on the sprint because of unplanned work.
I fell behind on code reviews this week due to on-call duties.
Don't fall behind on documentation — it compounds quickly.
The project fell behind after two team members went on leave.
If we fall behind now, it'll be hard to catch up before the release.

cards.meaning: To understand, solve, or find the answer to something
cards.examples:
I finally figured out why the tests were failing intermittently.
Can you figure out the root cause before our next sync?
She figured out the algorithm in under 30 minutes.
We need to figure out the data flow before writing any code.
I'm still trying to figure out how the caching layer works.

cards.meaning: To take further action after an initial step; to check on progress
cards.examples:
I'll follow up with the design team about the UI changes.
Did you follow up on the access request you sent last week?
Please follow up if you don't hear back by tomorrow.
She followed up after the interview and got the job.
Let's follow up on the action items from yesterday's meeting.

cards.meaning: To communicate an idea clearly and successfully
cards.examples:
I struggled to get my point across during the architecture discussion.
She got her concerns across without being confrontational.
Use diagrams to get complex ideas across more easily.
He couldn't get his explanation across, so he wrote it down.
A good presenter can get technical concepts across to non-engineers.

cards.meaning: To stop trying; to abandon an effort
cards.examples:
Don't give up on the fix — the solution is probably one line away.
She gave up trying to debug the third-party library.
We gave up on that approach after the proof of concept failed.
Never give up on writing clean code even under pressure.
He almost gave up on the project, but then had a breakthrough.

cards.meaning: To review, check, or explain something in detail
cards.examples:
Can we go over the pull request together before merging?
Let's go over the requirements one more time to avoid misunderstanding.
She went over the technical documentation before the interview.
I'll go over the code changes with you in the afternoon.
Could you go over the deployment steps with the new engineer?

cards.meaning: To delay or postpone an action
cards.examples:
Let's hold off on the release until the critical bug is fixed.
I held off on responding to the email until I had more information.
Can we hold off on refactoring until after the launch?
She held off on making a decision until she heard from the team.
Hold off on pushing that commit — the tests haven't passed yet.

cards.meaning: To stay at the same pace; to remain informed about something
cards.examples:
It's hard to keep up with the latest JavaScript frameworks.
She keeps up with all the sprint tickets by using a Kanban board.
How do you keep up with new developments in machine learning?
I follow a few newsletters to keep up with industry trends.
He struggled to keep up with the fast pace of the startup.

cards.meaning: To explain something clearly; to present or arrange details
cards.examples:
Can you lay out the pros and cons of each approach?
She laid out the entire architecture before writing a single line.
Let me lay out the plan for the next two sprints.
He laid out the steps clearly so the junior engineer could follow.
Please lay out your assumptions before presenting the estimate.

cards.meaning: To investigate or research a problem
cards.examples:
I'll look into why the API is returning a 500 error.
Can you look into the performance issues in the reporting module?
She looked into the new cloud pricing before switching providers.
We need to look into this customer complaint as soon as possible.
He looked into alternative database solutions over the weekend.

cards.meaning: To progress past a topic or difficulty; to start the next thing
cards.examples:
Let's move on to the next agenda item.
I think we've discussed this enough — time to move on.
She moved on from the rejected proposal and tried a different approach.
After the failed project, the team moved on with renewed focus.
Let's move on to the testing phase once code review is done.

cards.meaning: To reduce a list of options to a smaller set
cards.examples:
We need to narrow down the candidates to three before the final round.
Let's narrow down the root causes to make debugging faster.
She narrowed down the design options to two after user testing.
Can you narrow down the scope of this ticket before the sprint?
We narrowed down the tech stack choices to React and Vue.

cards.meaning: To learn casually without formal training; to collect or acquire
cards.examples:
I picked up TypeScript by working on a side project.
She picked up a lot of soft skills during her first year at work.
Can you pick up the slack while I'm on leave?
He picked up the basics of Docker in just a few days.
I need to pick up the printed reports before the presentation.

cards.meaning: To draw attention to something; to indicate or highlight
cards.examples:
She pointed out a critical edge case in the code review.
I want to point out that this issue was raised two sprints ago.
He pointed out the inconsistency in the API documentation.
The linter pointed out 12 unused variables in the codebase.
Can you point out where in the code this error is thrown?

cards.meaning: To succeed at something challenging or unlikely
cards.examples:
They pulled off the migration with zero downtime.
She pulled off a flawless product demo despite the last-minute changes.
I can't believe we pulled off that feature in just one sprint.
He pulled off a perfect score in the system design interview.
The team pulled off the launch against all odds.

cards.meaning: To postpone; to cause someone to lose interest or enthusiasm
cards.examples:
Don't put off writing tests — it creates technical debt.
She put off the difficult conversation for too long.
I keep putting off learning Kubernetes because it seems complex.
He was put off by the aggressive tone in the code review.
Let's not put off this discussion — it's blocking the whole team.

cards.meaning: To contact someone, especially to ask for help or offer support
cards.examples:
Feel free to reach out if you get stuck on the implementation.
She reached out to the vendor for clarification on the API docs.
I'll reach out to the stakeholders before making this change.
Please reach out to the security team before deploying this update.
He reached out to his network and found a job within two weeks.

cards.meaning: To encounter a problem or person unexpectedly
cards.examples:
We ran into a compatibility issue after the library upgrade.
I ran into my old colleague at the tech conference.
She ran into some trouble setting up the local development environment.
We keep running into the same issue with memory leaks.
He ran into a wall trying to integrate the two systems.

cards.meaning: To have no more of something left
cards.examples:
We're running out of time before the demo — focus on the core feature.
The team ran out of sprint capacity midway through the cycle.
I ran out of ideas for optimizing this query.
We ran out of storage space on the server.
She ran out of patience waiting for the deployment to finish.

cards.meaning: To reserve time, money, or resources for a specific purpose
cards.examples:
Set aside at least 20% of the sprint for technical debt.
She sets aside one hour each day for learning new skills.
We need to set aside a budget for the cloud migration.
I set aside time every Friday to write documentation.
Let's set aside this discussion and come back to it later.

cards.meaning: To establish, configure, or arrange something
cards.examples:
I'll set up the CI/CD pipeline by end of day.
Can you set up a meeting with the product team for tomorrow?
She set up the new developer's environment in under an hour.
We need to set up monitoring before we go live.
He set up automated alerts for any spike in error rates.

cards.meaning: To arrive or appear, especially unexpectedly or noticeably
cards.examples:
The bug only shows up in production, not locally.
She always shows up prepared with data to support her arguments.
Please show up on time for the client presentation.
The memory leak shows up after running the app for 24 hours.
He showed up to the retrospective with a detailed action plan.

cards.meaning: To resolve a problem or organize something that is in disorder
cards.examples:
Let me sort out the merge conflicts and get back to you.
Can you sort out the sprint board before the planning session?
She sorted out the billing issue with the cloud provider.
We need to sort out the team responsibilities before the project starts.
I'll sort out the access permissions for the new joiners today.

cards.meaning: To be noticeably different or better than others
cards.examples:
Your clean code and clear comments really stood out during the review.
She stood out in the interview because she asked excellent questions.
This feature will make our product stand out from competitors.
His communication skills stood out as much as his technical ability.
What makes you stand out as a candidate for this role?

cards.meaning: To accept a task, responsibility, or challenge
cards.examples:
I'm happy to take on the role of release manager this sprint.
She took on the most complex module in the project without hesitation.
Are you comfortable taking on this task given your current workload?
He took on the mentorship of two junior engineers.
We shouldn't take on new features until the backlog is cleared.

cards.meaning: To assume control or responsibility from someone else
cards.examples:
Can you take over the on-call shift for me on Friday?
She took over the project after the original lead resigned.
AI is slowly taking over repetitive tasks in the software industry.
He took over the meeting when the facilitator lost connection.
Please take over this ticket — I'll be tied up in interviews today.

cards.meaning: To briefly make contact with someone to share updates or check in
cards.examples:
Let's touch base after the standup to go over the design.
I'll touch base with the client once we have a preliminary answer.
She touched base with every team member before the quarterly review.
Can we touch base tomorrow morning before the sprint planning?
He touched base with the security team about the new feature.

cards.meaning: To find something or someone after a search
cards.examples:
I spent two hours trying to track down the source of the memory leak.
She tracked down the original author of the legacy code.
Can you track down the ticket where this decision was documented?
He tracked down the missing requirement by reviewing old meeting notes.
I finally tracked down the issue to a timezone conversion bug.

cards.meaning: To reverse a negative situation; to complete quickly
cards.examples:
The new team lead turned the struggling project around in two sprints.
Can you turn around a quick fix for this by end of day?
She turned around the client relationship with one honest conversation.
We turned the product around by focusing on user feedback.
He turned around a full report in just three hours.

cards.meaning: To explain something step by step in detail
cards.examples:
Can you walk me through the codebase before I start?
She walked the new joiner through the deployment process.
Let's walk through the user journey together to find the gap.
He walked us through his technical design in the architecture review.
Please walk me through how you arrived at this solution.

cards.meaning: To solve a problem; to result in a good outcome; to exercise
cards.examples:
I'm sure we can work out a solution that satisfies everyone.
It took three attempts, but we worked out the optimal algorithm.
Things worked out well after the last-minute refactor.
She works out before her shift to stay focused throughout the day.
I need to work out the edge cases before submitting the PR.

cards.meaning: To finish or conclude something; to summarize
cards.examples:
Let's wrap up the meeting — we're five minutes over.
I'll wrap up the remaining tasks before logging off.
She wrapped up the project documentation before her last day.
We're almost done — just need to wrap up the final testing.
Can you wrap up with a quick summary of the key decisions?

cards.meaning: To support a claim or person; to create a copy of data
cards.examples:
Always back up your database before running a migration.
Can you back up your estimate with some data?
She backed up the team's decision in front of the stakeholders.
Make sure to back up the config files before the system update.
He backed up his colleague when the manager questioned the approach.

cards.meaning: To stop working; to analyze or divide into smaller parts
cards.examples:
Let's break down this large ticket into smaller subtasks.
The legacy system finally broke down after years of neglect.
She broke down the complex algorithm into simple steps.
Can you break down the cost estimate by phase?
When things break down in production, stay calm and check the logs.

cards.meaning: To become exhausted from overwork and stress
cards.examples:
Many engineers burn out when they work long hours without rest.
She burned out after three months of on-call duties every week.
Take breaks to avoid burning out during intense project phases.
He burned out and took two weeks off to recover.
Managers should watch for signs of burnout in their team.

cards.meaning: To finally find time to do something you've been postponing
cards.examples:
I'll get around to reviewing your PR after this meeting.
I never got around to learning Docker Swarm before Kubernetes took over.
She finally got around to refactoring the authentication module.
When will you get around to finishing the documentation?
I keep meaning to get around to setting up my dev environment properly.

cards.meaning: To resolve small problems or smooth out difficulties
cards.examples:
We still need to iron out the edge cases in the payment flow.
Let's iron out the disagreement before the next sprint.
She ironed out the communication gaps between the frontend and backend teams.
We ironed out the last few bugs before the release.
Can we iron out the ambiguous requirements before estimation?

cards.meaning: To admire and respect someone as a role model
cards.examples:
I look up to engineers who write clean, well-documented code.
She looks up to her mentor who taught her how to handle tough conversations.
Junior developers look up to seniors who take time to explain things.
He looks up to open-source contributors who give back to the community.
I look up to people who can stay calm under pressure.

cards.meaning: To fail to experience or benefit from something
cards.examples:
Don't miss out on the knowledge transfer session — it's really useful.
She missed out on the promotion because she didn't speak up.
You'll miss out on a lot if you skip the code review process.
He missed out on early ownership because he joined the team late.
Don't miss out on networking opportunities at tech conferences.

cards.meaning: To share thoughts or feelings; to become available or possible
cards.examples:
It's important to open up about blockers early in the sprint.
She opened up about her concerns during the one-on-one meeting.
This technology opens up new possibilities for real-time collaboration.
He was hesitant to open up at first, but gradually became more vocal.
Opening up honest communication channels makes teams stronger.

cards.meaning: To increase effort; to take on more responsibility
cards.examples:
She stepped up and led the project when the team lead was absent.
We need someone to step up and own the deployment process.
He stepped up his contributions after the quarterly review feedback.
It's time to step up and tackle the most challenging problems.
The team stepped up under pressure and delivered on time.

cards.meaning: To focus closely on a specific detail or issue
cards.examples:
Let's zoom in on the bottleneck in the data pipeline.
She zoomed in on user feedback to identify the core pain point.
Zoom in on this part of the diagram — that's where the issue is.
We need to zoom in on what's causing the latency spike.
He zoomed in on the failing test case to understand the root cause.

cards.meaning: What you do is more important than what you say
cards.examples:
He promised to improve his delivery, but actions speak louder than words — let's see it in the next sprint.
In IELTS speaking: 'Actions speak louder than words — real change requires effort, not just promises.'
Don't just say you're a team player; actions speak louder than words.
Governments that claim to protect the environment must remember: actions speak louder than words.
She didn't make promises in the interview — she showed her portfolio, because actions speak louder than words.

cards.word: A stitch in time saves nine
cards.meaning: Fixing a small problem early prevents it from becoming a bigger one
cards.examples:
A stitch in time saves nine — fix that memory leak before it crashes production.
If we write tests now, we avoid major regressions later; a stitch in time saves nine.
In IELTS writing: 'As the saying goes, a stitch in time saves nine, and preventive healthcare is far cheaper than treatment.'
Address the technical debt this sprint — a stitch in time saves nine.
She caught the security flaw early; a stitch in time truly saves nine.

cards.meaning: Repeated effort and practice leads to improvement and mastery
cards.examples:
I keep doing mock interviews because practice makes perfect.
In IELTS speaking: 'Practice makes perfect, and language fluency is no exception.'
She improved her public speaking because she believed practice makes perfect.
Practice makes perfect — write code every day, even if it's small.
He repeated the algorithm problems until they felt natural; practice truly makes perfect.

cards.word: Don't judge a book by its cover
cards.meaning: Don't form an opinion based on appearance alone
cards.examples:
Don't judge a book by its cover — that junior engineer wrote the most elegant solution.
In IELTS: 'Society would benefit greatly if we stopped judging books by their covers.'
The old-looking codebase was actually brilliant inside — don't judge a book by its cover.
She seemed quiet in meetings, but don't judge a book by its cover — her work was outstanding.
Don't judge a book by its cover when hiring; focus on skills, not background.

cards.word: The early bird catches the worm
cards.meaning: Starting early gives you an advantage
cards.examples:
The early bird catches the worm — apply for that role before it closes.
She finished her IELTS prep early because the early bird catches the worm.
In writing: 'Entrepreneurs who act early thrive — the early bird always catches the worm.'
Start the sprint planning the day before — the early bird catches the worm.
He invested in cloud skills early in his career because the early bird catches the worm.

cards.word: Every cloud has a silver lining
cards.meaning: Every difficult situation has a positive aspect
cards.examples:
The project was cancelled, but every cloud has a silver lining — we learned a lot.
In IELTS speaking: 'Even during the pandemic, every cloud had a silver lining for remote work culture.'
The failed deployment taught us to automate rollbacks — every cloud has a silver lining.
She didn't get the promotion, but it pushed her to upskill; every cloud has a silver lining.
Every cloud has a silver lining — the criticism helped me write better code.

cards.word: Two heads are better than one
cards.meaning: Collaboration and working together produces better results
cards.examples:
Let's pair program on this — two heads are better than one.
In IELTS: 'Team projects encourage collaboration because two heads are better than one.'
She asked a colleague to review her design because two heads are better than one.
We brainstormed together and found a smarter solution; two heads are better than one.
In code reviews, two heads are better than one — bugs get caught faster.

cards.meaning: It is better to do something late than not to do it at all
cards.examples:
I finally wrote the unit tests — better late than never.
In IELTS: 'Starting to exercise in middle age is better late than never.'
He finally documented the API; better late than never.
She joined the team two weeks late, but better late than never — she made a big impact.
Better late than never — I finally got around to learning Git properly.

cards.word: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
cards.meaning: Avoid depending on a single option or plan
cards.examples:
Don't put all your eggs in one basket — back up to multiple storage regions.
In IELTS: 'Investing in a diverse skill set means you don't put all your eggs in one basket.'
Apply to multiple companies; don't put all your eggs in one basket.
She had a backup plan ready because she never puts all her eggs in one basket.
Diversify your tech stack — don't put all your eggs in one basket.

cards.word: Rome wasn't built in a day
cards.meaning: Important things take time and effort to build
cards.examples:
Be patient with your IELTS preparation — Rome wasn't built in a day.
In IELTS writing: 'Sustainable development is a long process; Rome was not built in a day.'
Our platform took three years to mature — Rome wasn't built in a day.
She didn't become a senior engineer overnight; Rome wasn't built in a day.
Don't rush the architecture — Rome wasn't built in a day, and neither is a good system.

cards.word: Where there's a will, there's a way
cards.meaning: If you are determined, you can find a way to achieve your goal
cards.examples:
I didn't know Kubernetes, but where there's a will, there's a way — I learned it in a month.
In IELTS: 'Where there's a will, there's a way — motivated students overcome resource limitations.'
The team had no prior experience in blockchain, but where there's a will, there's a way.
She passed the interview despite limited preparation — where there's a will, there's a way.
Where there's a will, there's a way; we shipped the feature despite the tight deadline.

cards.meaning: The results you get in life reflect the effort or actions you put in
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'You reap what you sow — consistent effort in education leads to long-term success.'
He invested in his team and they delivered brilliantly — you truly reap what you sow.
You reap what you sow: skip testing today and you'll debug crashes tomorrow.
She worked hard for years, and the recognition came — you reap what you sow.
You reap what you sow in relationships; treat colleagues well and you'll build a strong network.

cards.meaning: Having information and education gives you an advantage
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'Knowledge is power, and access to quality education is essential for equality.'
Knowledge is power — the more you understand the codebase, the faster you can debug.
She reads widely because she believes knowledge is power.
In the information age, knowledge is power — digital literacy is a critical skill.
Knowledge is power; the more you understand about the system, the more influence you have.

cards.meaning: Avoid damaging important relationships that may be useful in the future
cards.examples:
Even if you're leaving the company, don't burn your bridges — the tech world is small.
In IELTS: 'Professional relationships matter; it's wise to never burn your bridges.'
She left her previous job gracefully because she knew not to burn her bridges.
He gave honest but respectful feedback so as not to burn his bridges.
Don't burn your bridges over a disagreement — you may work with them again.

cards.word: Strike while the iron is hot
cards.meaning: Take advantage of an opportunity before it passes
cards.examples:
The client is interested right now — let's strike while the iron is hot and close the deal.
In IELTS: 'Entrepreneurs should strike while the iron is hot when new markets emerge.'
Apply for the job now — strike while the iron is hot before it's filled.
She got an introduction to the CTO and followed up immediately — she knew to strike while the iron is hot.
Strike while the iron is hot and deploy the fix while the system is in maintenance mode.

cards.word: The pen is mightier than the sword
cards.meaning: Written words and ideas have more power than physical force
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'The pen is mightier than the sword — journalism has toppled more regimes than armies.'
The pen is mightier than the sword; a well-written email can resolve what a heated meeting cannot.
She chose to write a detailed report rather than argue — the pen is mightier than the sword.
In software, good documentation is power — the pen is mightier than the sword.
History shows the pen is mightier than the sword — ideas outlast empires.

cards.word: All that glitters is not gold
cards.meaning: Not everything that looks good or attractive is valuable
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'All that glitters is not gold — social media success doesn't reflect true happiness.'
That new framework looks great, but all that glitters is not gold — check the community support.
He learned that all that glitters is not gold after taking a high-salary job with a toxic culture.
The startup had great branding, but all that glitters is not gold — their product had serious flaws.
In interviews, all that glitters is not gold; evaluate the culture, not just the salary.

cards.word: Too many cooks spoil the broth
cards.meaning: Having too many people involved in something can make it worse
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'Committee decisions can be slow and ineffective — too many cooks spoil the broth.'
We had seven people in the design meeting and nothing got decided — too many cooks spoil the broth.
Assign clear ownership to tasks; too many cooks spoil the broth in complex projects.
She limited the code reviewers to two — too many cooks spoil the broth.
Too many cooks spoil the broth: keep your core decision-making team small.

cards.word: Necessity is the mother of invention
cards.meaning: When people truly need something, they will find a way to create it
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'Necessity is the mother of invention — most breakthrough technologies emerged from critical problems.'
We had no budget for a third-party tool, so we built our own — necessity is the mother of invention.
The pandemic forced schools to innovate online; necessity truly is the mother of invention.
She built the monitoring dashboard herself out of need — necessity is the mother of invention.
Great startups solve real problems because necessity is the mother of invention.

cards.word: Don't count your chickens before they hatch
cards.meaning: Don't assume success before it is certain
cards.examples:
Don't count your chickens before they hatch — wait for the client's written confirmation.
In IELTS: 'Investors should not count their chickens before they hatch when entering volatile markets.'
The deployment looked smooth, but don't count your chickens before they hatch until monitoring confirms it.
She was celebrating too early — she shouldn't count her chickens before they hatch.
Don't count your chickens before they hatch; always have a contingency plan.

cards.meaning: Some situations or problems require the cooperation of two parties
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'Conflict resolution requires effort from both sides — it takes two to tango.'
It takes two to tango — both the frontend and backend need to agree on the API contract.
Don't blame only one side; it takes two to tango.
Successful stakeholder alignment takes two to tango — the team and the client both need to compromise.
She reminded her colleague that it takes two to tango when discussing communication failures.

cards.word: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link
cards.meaning: A system or team is only as effective as its least capable part
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'A team is only as strong as its weakest link — investing in every member's growth is vital.'
A chain is only as strong as its weakest link — that's why code quality standards apply to everyone.
She made sure even junior team members were well-supported because a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
In security, a chain is only as strong as its weakest link — one vulnerability can compromise everything.
Support the struggling team member; a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

cards.word: The squeaky wheel gets the grease
cards.meaning: The person or thing that makes the most noise gets attention
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'In democracies, the squeaky wheel gets the grease — vocal communities get better services.'
In open-source, the squeaky wheel gets the grease — file that bug report and follow up.
She raised the issue repeatedly because the squeaky wheel gets the grease.
He learned that in corporate environments, the squeaky wheel gets the grease — speak up for your team.
If your ticket isn't moving, comment on it — the squeaky wheel gets the grease.

cards.meaning: Think carefully before taking action to avoid making mistakes
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'Look before you leap — major life decisions should be made after careful thought.'
Look before you leap when switching to a new technology without testing it thoroughly.
She researched the company thoroughly because she believes in looking before you leap.
Don't merge that PR without reading it — look before you leap.
Look before you leap: a hasty refactor can break more than it fixes.

cards.word: The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago; the second best time is now
cards.meaning: It's never too late to start something important — act now
cards.examples:
In IELTS: 'The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago; the second best time is now — start investing in education today.'
I wish I'd started learning English earlier, but the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago — the second best is now.
Start writing tests today; the best time was when the project began, but the second best time is now.
She started her fitness journey at 35 — the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago; the second best is now.
Begin your IELTS preparation today; the second best time to start is always now.
